sentences.text: Monday at Contoso.
Over the weekend, the maker rewrote the instructions of Nexo, the I T agent, and ran the test set again.
Monday morning, twelve cases are red.
The first instinct is to rewrite the instructions again, and run again, and hope.
But the real cause is not in the instructions at all.
Today you learn to read the results before you change anything.
Keep this picture.
Reading results is like reviewing a graded exam.
You don't only look at the score.
You ask three questions.
What result did each answer get?
Why did it get that result?
And did this exam improve compared with the last one?
Copilot Studio gives you one tool for each question: the result itself, the activity map, and Compare with.
Every case gets one of four results.
Pass and Fail are the grades you expect: the method judged the answer.
Invalid means the case is missing what the method needs, like an expected response, keywords, or tools.
Error means an execution failure while evaluating, so there is no grade at all.
Only Pass and Fail say something about the answer.
Invalid and Error tell you to look at the run first.
Your turn.
Contoso raises the Compare meaning pass score to ninety five.
Cases that have an expected response now score below that bar.
What result do those cases get?
Invalid, because the bar is too demanding?
Error, because the method could not decide?
Or Fail, because they scored below the bar?
Decide before I answer.
Fail.
The case had everything the method needs, so it was graded.
Invalid is only for missing material.
When one case confuses you, open Show activity map.
It shows the sequence of decisions Nexo made in that case, step by step, until it answered.
Here, the user asked how to reconnect the V P N, and the map shows Nexo went to the Password reset topic first.
Now you know why the answer was wrong, instead of guessing.
To measure a change, use Compare with.
It puts two runs of the same test set side by side.
Arrows mark the cases that changed, from failing to passing, or the other way around.
Contoso edits the instructions, runs the same set again, and sees five cases improve and one get worse.
That one is the next case to open.
Compare with only makes sense on the same test set.
Results do not stay forever.
Copilot Studio keeps evaluation results for eighty nine days.
To keep them longer, export them to a C S V file.
Each row has the question, the expected response, the method, the score, the agent's response, the result, and the analysis.
That file is your history, for audits and for comparisons months later.
Your turn.
Contoso's auditors want this quarter's evaluation results available for a full year.
What should the maker do?
Export the results to C S V after each run?
Ask an admin to extend the result retention?
Or use Compare with to merge the older runs?
Decide before I answer.
Export to C S V.
Results stay eighty nine days, and exporting is how you keep them longer.
Compare with only puts two runs side by side.
Everything so far is the standard harness.
On the Microsoft Copilot harness, formerly GitHub Copilot harness, results live in the Evaluate tab.
Each run is saved separately.
To run a set again, open Recent results, then Evaluate test set again.
The summary shows Score, Duration, Test cases, Data type, User profile, and Credits used.
Duration is the whole run, not how fast the agent answered.
Measure latency in Preview.
On this harness, a fail can come from three places.
The evaluation setup, owned by the evaluation author.
The agent configuration, owned by the agent builder.
Or a platform limitation, owned by the platform team.
Check the setup first.
Are the dependencies healthy?
Is the authentication valid for the user profile?
Is it the right environment?
Only then blame the agent.
Your turn.
Back to Monday.
Twelve cases fail overnight.
All of them call the Create Ticket tool, and the connection for the user profile expired yesterday.
What should the maker do first?
Rewrite the instructions and run the set again?
Restore the connection and rerun the same set?
Or improve the Create Ticket tool description?
Decide before I answer.
Restore the connection and rerun.
An expired connection is a setup issue.
Leave the instructions alone.
When the agent really is the cause, match the symptom to the fix.
Low General quality means improve the instructions.
Missing or incorrect tool use means improve the tool descriptions.
Incorrect information means check the knowledge sources.
Change one thing, run the same set again, and use Compare with to see the effect.
With many failures, you need an order.
First, safety and compliance.
Then the core business scenarios, the ones Contoso cannot work without.
Then the lowest scoring evaluation.
Last, the failures that keep coming back.
A low score on the cafeteria menu can wait.
An answer that breaks a privacy rule cannot.
Your turn.
After a run, Nexo has three failures.
A vague answer about the cafeteria menu, a wrong order status, and an answer that shares an employee's home address.
Which one do you triage first?
The wrong order status in a core scenario?
The vague menu answer with the lowest score?
Or the answer sharing an employee's address?
Decide before I answer.
The shared address.
Safety and compliance come first, then core scenarios.
One last number: credits.
Evaluation runs use Copilot Credits.
The credits you see in Evaluate and in Preview are estimates, close to real time.
The final, accurate consumption appears in the Monitor tab within a few hours, after the usage is processed.
So for the real number, check Monitor later, not the run summary.
Back to Monday.
The maker leaves the instructions alone, restores the connection, and runs the same set again.
Compare with shows the twelve cases going from fail to pass.
Remember for the exam.
Four results: Pass, Fail, Invalid, Error.
A demanding pass score gives Fail, not Invalid.
Activity map explains one case.
Compare with measures a change.
Eighty nine days, then C S V.
Check the setup first, and triage safety first.
